title: openinterpreter/openinterpreter — A coding agent for open models like Kimi K3
content:
A coding agent optimized for low-cost models. Blog post ↗
Note
Today: Kimi K3 is here. We have reimplemented the provider-recommended Kimi Code harness in Rust, giving you maximum K3 performance with a Codex-like interface. Kimi Docs →
macOS and Linux:
curl -fsSL https://www.openinterpreter.com/install | sh
Windows:
irm https://www.openinterpreter.com/install.ps1 | iex
Then type i or interpreter in your terminal to start a session.
Open Interpreter is a fork of OpenAI's Codex, with a focus on emulating the agent harness that gets the best performance out of low-cost models.
Use /harness to switch the active harness:
> /harness
native
claude-code
claude-code-bare
zcode
kimi-code
kimi-cli
qwen-code
deepseek-tui
swe-agent
minimal
Read more in the harness docs and provider setup guides.
Open Interpreter works in ACP-compatible editors and clients. Configure the client to launch interpreter acp; see the ACP guide for examples.
Already building with OpenAI's Codex SDK? Keep the SDK and make a one-line binary override:
-const codex = new Codex();
+const codex = new Codex({ codexPathOverride: "interpreter" });
Open Interpreter speaks the same Codex exec protocol. See the SDK guide and run scripts/test-codex-sdk-compat.sh for a local, provider-free compatibility check.
Open Interpreter should fit into your existing agent setup instead of trapping it in an Open Interpreter-only format. The product goal is to prefer shared, tool-neutral standards and directories, keep user-authored data in readable files, and make moving to or from another compatible agent straightforward.
Today that includes repository AGENTS.md, shared .agents/skills directories,
MCP, ACP, and the Codex exec protocol. Product-specific storage under
~/.openinterpreter is reserved for configuration and runtime state that does
not yet have a practical shared standard. Legacy product-specific skill
directories remain readable for compatibility, but new skills belong in
.agents/skills or ~/.agents/skills.
See the portability guide for the current boundary and the rules for evolving it.
Open Interpreter ships with a QA skill that lets any model operate and test interfaces. It can drive web apps in a real browser with agent-browser, or operate and test native apps with trycua.
- Runs commands inside native sandboxing on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
- Switches providers and models from the TUI with /model .
- Inspects or switches Rust-native model harnesses with /harness .
- Tests web and native apps through the built-in QA skill.
- Runs as an Agent Client Protocol agent for editors with interpreter acp .
- Reuses shared AGENTS.md instructions and.agents/skills directories.
- Keeps product-only config and session state local under ~/.openinterpreter .
- Supports exec , MCP, skills, hooks, permissions, andAGENTS.md .
Provider and model membership is generated, not maintained as Rust lists. From
codex-rs, refresh all hosted providers with
python3 scripts/write_provider_catalog.py, or repeat
--provider <provider-id> to update only selected provider entries. Live model
sources require the provider credentials documented in the
provider docs.
Note
This is the new Rust version of Open Interpreter, based on Codex. Looking for the original Python project? It lives on as a community-maintained fork at endolith/open-interpreter.
Apache-2.0

report.summary: Open Interpreter is now a Rust-based coding agent for low-cost open models like Kimi K3, built as a portable fork of OpenAI Codex.
report.background: Open Interpreter began as a Python tool that lets natural language drive code execution. It has now been rewritten in Rust as a fork of OpenAI's Codex, with a focus on getting strong performance out of inexpensive and open-weight models. The immediate catalyst is the release of Kimi K3: the project reimplemented Kimi's provider-recommended coding harness natively in Rust, exposing a Codex-like interface. More broadly, the AI coding agent space is shifting toward cost-conscious, model-agnostic workflows. Developers want to switch between Claude, Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, and other models without being locked into a vendor-specific harness. Open Interpreter leans into this by supporting multiple harnesses and open protocols like MCP, ACP, AGENTS.md, and the Codex exec protocol. The original Python project continues as a community-maintained fork.
key_points: Rust rewrite for performance: Open Interpreter has been rebuilt in Rust on top of OpenAI's Codex codebase, replacing the original Python implementation. The new binary installs with a single command and starts a session by typing `i` or `interpreter`. Its immediate focus is maximizing Kimi K3's performance through a natively reimplemented, provider-recommended harness.

Switchable harnesses: The `/harness` command lets users cycle through multiple agent harnesses, including native, claude-code, zcode, kimi-code, qwen-code, deepseek-tui, swe-agent, and minimal. This lets one agent adapt to the prompt and tool-use styles that work best for each specific model, which is critical when using low-cost models instead of relying on a single proprietary system.

Designed for interoperability, not lock-in: Open Interpreter deliberately uses shared, tool-neutral standards: AGENTS.md for instructions, `.agents/skills` for reusable skills, plus MCP, ACP, and the Codex exec protocol. It can be dropped into existing OpenAI Codex SDK setups via a one-line `codexPathOverride`, and users can move to or from other compatible agents without rewriting their data.

Built-in QA skill: A QA skill lets any model operate and test interfaces. It can drive web apps in a real browser using agent-browser, or test native applications through trycua. Commands run inside native sandboxing on macOS, Linux, and Windows, making the agent capable of verifying its own work in safe environments.

Automated provider catalog: Provider and model listings are generated from codex-rs rather than maintained by hand, using a script that refreshes all hosted providers or just selected ones. Live model sources require provider credentials, but this approach keeps the tool current as new models like Kimi K3 appear without waiting for a manual update.
report.impact: This project underscores a broader industry move toward open-weight models and cost-efficient coding agents. By emulating the best harness for each provider and supporting shared protocols, Open Interpreter lowers the barrier to switching models and avoids vendor lock-in. Developers get a familiar Codex-compatible interface that works with existing SDKs, while being able to experiment with Kimi K3, Qwen, DeepSeek, and others at lower cost. The focus on AGENTS.md and portable skill directories helps teams standardize agent behavior across tools. For everyday users, the built-in QA skill and sandboxing mean coding agents can safely test applications, potentially making autonomous coding assistance more reliable and accessible beyond just those who can afford expensive flagship models.
report.tools: Try the main repo: github.com/openinterpreter/openinterpreter. For the original Python version, see the community fork github.com/endolith/open-interpreter. Follow Kimi K3 docs at platform.moonshot.ai. For testing, explore agent-browser and trycua. MCP and ACP specs are useful for integrating with editors and other agents.
